mainTopic: How judges are chosen for דיני ממונות, and when a litigant may reject the other side's judges or witnesses.
overview: The משנה teaches that a money case is judged by three judges. רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about who picks the third judge, and whether a litigant can reject the other side's judges or witnesses. The גמרא first tries reading 'one' as a whole court, and deals with a borrower's right to refuse a court. Then it drops that reading: each side picks one judge and a third is added, so that a true judgment comes out. Next it explains the argument over the third judge. Everyone needs the judges to agree, and they argue only about whether the litigants must agree too. Along the way it supports רב יהודה's rule that witnesses sign only when they know who signs with them. Finally, רבי יוחנן limits rejecting judges to lay courts, and the גמרא defends this against several challenges. This leads to ריש לקיש's reading 'his witness' and the question of backing out of accepting one witness like two, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Three judges, and how they are chosen
steps.stepSummary: דיני ממונות need three judges. Each litigant picks one judge. רבי מאיר says the two litigants pick the third, and חכמים say the two chosen judges pick the third.
steps.simpleTranslation: Money cases are judged by three. Each side picks one judge. רבי מאיר says the two litigants together pick a third. חכמים say the two judges pick the third.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the chapter by setting the number of judges for money cases at three. It then gives a מחלוקת about who chooses the third judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that each litigant picks one judge. The only argument is about the third judge. רבי מאיר gives that choice to the litigants, and חכמים give it to the two judges who were already chosen.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Monetary cases are judged by three.
This litigant chooses one for himself,
and that litigant chooses one for himself,
and the two of them choose one more for themselves;
these are the words of רבי מאיר.
And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי דַיָּינִין בּוֹרְרִין לָהֶן עוֹד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: The two judges choose one more for themselves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening of the chapter's משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three judges sit on a money case and each litigant picks one. רבי מאיר says the litigants pick the third, and חכמים say the two judges pick the third.

steps.title: Rejecting the other side's judge
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says each litigant can reject the judge the other side chose. חכמים say he can do so only by proving the judge is a relative or otherwise פסול, and never if the judge is כשר or a court-approved expert.
steps.simpleTranslation: Each side may reject the other's judge, says רבי מאיר. חכמים ask: when? Only when he brings proof that the judges are relatives or unfit. If they are fit, or experts approved by the court, he cannot reject them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second מחלוקת. This one is about whether a litigant can reject the judge his opponent chose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר states the right to reject without adding a condition. חכמים limit it: you need proof of a real disqualification, such as being a relative. Without proof, a fit judge or a מומחה approved by the court cannot be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: Relatives, who are not allowed to judge

phrases.english: This litigant can disqualify the judge of that one,
and that litigant can disqualify the judge of this one —
these are the words of רבי מאיר.
And the Sages say: When is this so?
When he brings proof about them
that they are relatives or unfit.
But if they were fit
or experts approved by the court —
he cannot disqualify them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a second מחלוקת about the chosen judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר says a litigant can reject the other side's judge. חכמים say this works only with proof that the judge is a relative or פסול, and never against a fit judge or a court-approved expert.

steps.title: Rejecting the other side's witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The same מחלוקת applies to witnesses. רבי מאיר says each side can reject the other's witnesses, and חכמים require proof that they are relatives or פסולים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Each side may reject the other's witnesses, says רבי מאיר. חכמים ask: when? Only when he brings proof that they are relatives or unfit. If they are fit, he cannot reject them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה repeats the same pattern, this time for עדים instead of judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The structure matches the previous step word for word. One phrase is missing here: 'experts approved by the court'. That idea applies only to judges, not to witnesses.
steps.whatToRemember: In all three cases, everyone agrees that each side picks one judge. רבי מאיר gives the litigants more power to pick and to reject. חכמים limit rejection to cases with proof of a real disqualification.

phrases.english: This litigant can disqualify the witnesses of that one,
and that litigant can disqualify the witnesses of this one.
These are the words of רבי מאיר.
And the Sages say: When is this so?
When he brings proof about them
that they are relatives or unfit,
but if they were fit —
he cannot disqualify them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same מחלוקת from judges to witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר says a litigant can reject the other side's witnesses. חכמים say only with proof that they are relatives or פסולים.

steps.title: Why does each side need to pick one, if three are enough?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the משנה's wording. Why does each side need to pick 'one', when three judges are enough to judge the case?
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: What does 'this one chooses one and that one chooses one' mean? Three is enough!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by challenging the wording of the משנה. It sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא seems to read 'one' as a whole court of three for each side, which would add up to many judges. It objects that the opening line already said three judges are enough. So why would so many be needed?

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question about how three judges are picked. It shows that the גמרא is reading 'one' as a whole court, which is why it asks whether three judges are not already enough.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the meaning of "this one chooses one for himself
and that one chooses one for himself"?
phrases.notes: The גמרא seems to understand "one" as one whole court of three judges, not one single judge.

phrases.english: Three are enough!
phrases.notes: This points back to the opening line of the משנה: money cases need only three judges.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי זֶה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ אֶחָד וְזֶה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ אֶחָד בִּתְלָתָא סַגִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first line of the משנה and challenges how it is worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's phrase 'זה בורר לו אחד וזה בורר לו אחד'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If each 'one' is a whole court, there would be extra judges. But the משנה itself says three judges are enough for a money case.

steps.title: The משנה Means Each Side Picks a Whole Court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the משנה's 'one' as one בית דין of three judges, not one judge. When each side picks a different court, the two of them must agree on another court.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה means: when this litigant picks one court and that litigant picks a different court, the two of them together choose one more court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 4 by explaining what the משנה really means by 'one'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 already read 'one' as a whole court, and asked why so many judges would be needed. The answer is that the two courts do not sit together. Each one is only a proposal. When the two sides propose different courts, neither wins automatically, so they must agree on another court together, and that single court of three judges the case.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means. The גמרא is explaining the real meaning of a text.
One court, here meaning a full panel of three judges

steps.confusionAlert: The courts each side picks do not sit together to make one big panel. Each is only a proposal. In the end, one court of three judges the case, which is why the question 'three is enough' goes away.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
phrases.notes: The 'it' is the משנה from Step 1.

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֶׁזֶּה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ בֵּית דִּין אֶחָד,
phrases.english: When this one chooses for himself one court,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ בֵּית דִּין אֶחָד,
phrases.english: and that one chooses for himself one court,
the two of them choose for themselves one more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 4 by reading the wording of the משנה differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each side's court of three would sit together with the jointly chosen court, which would make far more than the three judges a money case needs.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each side proposes a full court, and the proposals are alternatives. When the two sides disagree, they jointly choose another court, and only that one court of three judges the case.

steps.title: Can a Borrower Really Refuse the Court?
steps.stepSummary: The new reading means a לוה could block the lender's court. That seems to contradict רבי אלעזר, who says only the מלוה can refuse and the borrower is forced to be judged in his own city.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can even the borrower block the choice of court? But רבי אלעזר said, about a different teaching, that the right to refuse a court was taught only about the lender. The borrower is forced to be judged in his own city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading from Step 5, because it lets the borrower refuse a court too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 5 both sides seem equal, so either one can reject the other's court. רבי אלעזר limits that right to the מלוה. The לוה is forced to accept the court in his own city. So how can the משנה give the borrower the same right?

phrases.english: And can even a borrower block it?
But didn't Rabbi Elazar say:
They taught this only about a lender,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the right to refuse a court, which the משנה gives.

phrases.english: but a borrower, they force him
and he is judged in his own city.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ לֹוֶה מָצֵי מְעַכֵּב? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the result of the answer in Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in Step 5, which lets either litigant refuse the other's court
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר limits the right to refuse to the מלוה. The לוה is forced to accept the local court, which contradicts a borrower blocking the lender's choice.

steps.title: The משנה Speaks of Lay Courts in Syria
steps.stepSummary: Borrowing רבי יוחנן's phrase, the גמרא says the משנה is about lay courts in Syria. There even a borrower may refuse. A court of experts may not be refused.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said, 'they taught it about the lay courts in Syria.' Here too, the משנה was taught about the lay courts in Syria. But if the lender chose expert judges, the borrower cannot refuse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the משנה to a particular kind of court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two rulings speak about different courts. Lay courts are not expert judges, so even a borrower may say he does not want them. When the court is made up of experts, רבי אלעזר's rule applies and the borrower must accept it.

keyTerms.meaning: Courts. Here it means lay courts, not expert judges.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yochanan said:
They taught it about the lay courts in Syria.
Here too,
they taught it about the lay courts in Syria.
But experts, no.
phrases.notes: If the lender picked expert judges, the borrower can't refuse them.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בְּעַרְכָּאוֹת שֶׁבְּסוּרְיָא שָׁנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 6 by narrowing the case in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower's right to refuse seemed to clash with רבי אלעזר.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower may refuse only lay courts. With expert courts, רבי אלעזר's rule stands.

steps.title: רב פפא: Even Expert Courts in the Same Town
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the משנה can even mean expert courts, such as those of רב הונא and רב חסדא. Either side can say, 'Am I putting you to any trouble?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: you can even say the משנה means expert courts, such as the courts of רב הונא and רב חסדא. There one side can say to the other, 'Am I troubling you?'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a different answer to the challenge in Step 6, so the משנה does not have to be limited to lay courts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר's rule keeps a borrower from being dragged to another place. When two expert courts are in the same town, choosing one over the other puts no extra burden on anyone. So either side may hold out for the court he prefers.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say. This opens a broader answer.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers. The first says the משנה is about lay courts, which even a borrower may refuse. רב פפא says it can even be about expert courts in the same town, where neither side burdens the other.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב פפא shows what lies behind רבי אלעזר's rule: a borrower may not refuse only when his choice would put a real burden on the other side.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
You can even say experts,

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן בֵּי דִינָא דְּרַב הוּנָא וּדְרַב חִסְדָּא,
phrases.english: such as the court of Rav Huna and that of Rav Chisda,
where he can say to him:
Am I troubling you?
phrases.notes: He means: both courts are right here, so picking the other one costs you nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מוּמְחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to Step 6, broader than the one in Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative case setting, with the reason behind the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Expert courts seemed to leave the borrower no right to refuse.
steps.terutzMaskana: With two local expert courts, refusing one puts no burden on anyone, so the borrower may refuse.

steps.title: The Rabbis' wording does not fit the 'court' reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the חכמים in the משנה, 'the two judges choose one more.' If each 'one' were a whole court, the two rejected courts would be choosing another court, which makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: the חכמים say the two judges pick one more. If you think each side picked a whole court, as we said before, then after those courts were rejected, do they go and pick another court?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reading from step 5, which said 'one' means one בית דין. It uses the חכמים's words in the משנה as the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים speak of 'two judges' who pick a third. Under the court reading, those 'two' would be two whole courts that the litigants already rejected. It is strange for rejected courts to go and pick a new court, so the court reading looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages say (the second opinion in the משנה)
If it enters your mind (if you were to think)

phrases.english: We learned: And the Rabbis say,

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי דַיָּינִין בּוֹרְרִין לָהֶן עוֹד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: the two judges choose one more for themselves.
And if it enters your mind
as we said, a court,
phrases.notes: This points back to step 5, where each side's 'one' was read as a full court of three.

phrases.english: then the courts, after they were disqualified,

phrases.aramaic: אָזְלוּ וּבָרְרוּ לְהוּ בֵּי דִינָא אַחֲרִינֵי?
phrases.english: go and choose another court for themselves?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים, שְׁנֵי דַיָּינִין בּוֹרְרִין לָהֶן עוֹד אֶחָד. וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the 'one court' reading from step 5 and challenges it from the חכמים's words.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 5, that 'one' means one בית דין of three.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים speak of 'two judges' picking a third. Under the court reading, these would be two rejected courts picking yet another court, which is unreasonable.

steps.title: A second problem with the 'court' reading
steps.stepSummary: A further challenge: the משנה's words 'this one chooses one and that one chooses one' do not fit the idea of each side picking a whole court.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, what does 'this one picks one and that one picks one' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second challenge to the court reading. This time it uses the משנה's own description of how the choosing works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the court reading, each side picks a court and then the other side rejects it. That would mean the normal method is built around each side rejecting the other's choice. The plain words 'each picks one' do not describe such a process, so the court reading seems forced.

keyTerms.meaning: This one chooses one for himself

phrases.english: And furthermore, what is meant by
"this one chooses one for himself
and that one chooses one for himself"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד, מַאי ״זֶה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ אֶחָד וְזֶה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ אֶחָד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, separate challenge to the same court reading attacked in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 5, that 'one' means one בית דין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה presents 'each picks one' as the normal method. It would be odd for the normal method to be each side picking a court only to have it rejected.

steps.title: Back to the plain reading: one judge each, plus a third
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the court reading. The משנה means each side picks one judge, and then the two of them pick one more judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what the משנה means: when one side picks one judge and the other side picks one judge, the two of them pick one more.
steps.whatsHappening: The word אלא tells us the גמרא is giving up the court reading because of the two challenges. It goes back to the simple meaning: three individual judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each litigant picks a single judge, and a third judge is added to make a court of three. This answers the question from step 4, since the three judges together are the court. Both challenges from steps 9 and 10 disappear, because no one is rejecting whole courts.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is saying

steps.whatToRemember: Final reading of the משנה: each side picks one judge, and a third judge is added. Together they make a court of three.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 5. The idea that 'one' means a whole court is now dropped. Here 'one' means one judge.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it is saying:
When this one chooses one judge for himself,
and that one chooses one judge for himself,
the two of them choose one more for themselves.
phrases.notes: This is the first view in the משנה. The חכמים said the two chosen judges pick the third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives up the court reading because of the challenges in steps 9 and 10, and goes back to the plain meaning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the משנה (dropping the earlier interpretation)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One' meant one court of three judges.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'One' means one judge. Each side picks one, and a third is added to make three.

steps.title: Why pick the judges this way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what is special about this method of choosing judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special here, that they do it this way?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the method is clear, the גמרא asks for its reason. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not about what the method is, but why we use it. Any three fit judges could make a court, so why have each side pick one?

keyTerms.meaning: What is different / what is special
That they do it this way

phrases.english: What is different, that they do it this way?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling what the method is in step 11, the גמרא now asks why.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the judges are picked one by each side, plus a third.

steps.title: So that a true judgment comes out
steps.stepSummary: The sages of ארץ ישראל, in the name of רבי זירא, explain: when each side picks a judge and a third is added, the judgment will come out true.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ארץ ישראל they said in the name of רבי זירא: because each side picks one judge and then the two pick one more, the judgment will come out true.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 12. The reason for the method is that it leads to a true judgment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When each litigant has a say in who the judges are, the process feels fair to both of them. That fairness helps the ruling be true and accepted. So the method is not just a technical detail; it serves the goal of real justice.

keyTerms.meaning: The judgment will come out true

steps.whatToRemember: Each side picks a judge so that a true and fair judgment will come out (רבי זירא).
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the method of picking judges exists for real justice, not only as a formal rule.

phrases.english: They say in the West in the name of רבי זירא:
phrases.notes: 'The West' is the גמרא's usual name for ארץ ישראל.

phrases.aramaic: מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁזֶּה בּוֹרֵר לוֹ דַּיָּין אֶחָד,
phrases.english: Because this one chooses one judge for himself,
and that one chooses one judge for himself,
and the two of them choose one more for themselves,
the judgment will come out true.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question from step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The method is used so that a true judgment will come out.

steps.title: Suggesting what the argument depends on
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the חכמים in the משנה and suggests that their argument with רבי מאיר depends on a rule of רב יהודה in the name of רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: the two judges choose the third. Shall we say the two sides argue about a rule that רב יהודה said in the name of רב?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It suggests that the argument in the משנה depends on a known rule, which it will quote in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the גמרא explained how the judges are picked. Now it asks what idea makes רבי מאיר and the חכמים disagree about who picks the third judge. The suggestion is that they disagree about רב יהודה's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (a suggestion the גמרא may later reject)
and the Sages say (quoting the משנה)

phrases.english: And the Sages say, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: the two judges who were chosen pick one more judge.

phrases.aramaic: נֵימָא בִּדְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב קָמִיפַּלְגִי?
phrases.english: Shall we say they disagree about what רב יהודה said in the name of רב?

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא בִּדְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining the method of choosing judges, the גמרא now looks for the reason behind the argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים depend on רב יהודה's rule?

steps.title: The rule of רב יהודה and how it would fit each side
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: witnesses do not sign a שטר unless they know who is signing with them. On this suggestion, רבי מאיר does not accept this rule and the חכמים do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: witnesses do not sign a document unless they know who signs with them. So רבי מאיר does not hold of this rule, and the חכמים do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רב יהודה's rule and shows how the suggested argument would work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person should only join a signature, or a court, together with people he knows are fit. The חכמים would say the two judges choose the third because they must know who sits with them. רבי מאיר, who lets each side be involved in choosing, would not hold of this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: he does not hold of (this rule)

phrases.english: As רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
Witnesses do not sign on a document

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יוֹדְעִין מִי חוֹתֵם עִמָּהֶן.
phrases.english: unless they know who is signing with them.
phrases.notes: He means they know the other signer is fit to be a witness.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר לֵית לֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: רבי מאיר does not hold of what רב יהודה said in the name of רב,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּנַן אִית לְהוּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב.
phrases.english: and the Sages do hold of what רב יהודה said in the name of רב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the rule named in step 14 and fits it to each side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses do not sign a שטר unless they know who signs with them; the suggestion is that the חכמים accept this and רבי מאיר does not.

steps.title: Everyone accepts the rule; the argument is about the litigants' consent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone accepts רב יהודה's rule and agrees the judges must approve. They argue only about whether the בעלי דינים must also approve.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone holds of רב יהודה's rule. Everyone agrees we need the judges to agree. They argue about the litigants: רבי מאיר says we also need the litigants to agree. The חכמים say we need the judges to agree, but not the litigants.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the suggestion and gives a new explanation of what the argument is really about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree the judges must know and accept the third judge. רבי מאיר adds that the בעלי דינים must also agree, so they are involved in choosing him. The חכמים say the judges' agreement is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: the litigants, the two sides in the case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי מאיר ignores the judges. He needs the judges to agree too. He just adds that the litigants must agree as well.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides need the judges to agree on the third judge. They argue only about whether the litigants must also agree.

phrases.aramaic: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: No, everyone holds of what רב יהודה said in the name of רב,
and as for the agreement of the judges,
everyone agrees that we need it.
Where they argue is the agreement of the litigants:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבַר דַּעַת בַּעֲלֵי דִינִין נָמֵי בָּעֵינַן,
phrases.english: רבי מאיר holds we need the agreement of the litigants too,
and the Sages hold we need the agreement of the judges,
but we do not need the agreement of the litigants.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of steps 14-15 and explains the argument another way.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the idea that the argument depends on רב יהודה's rule. It does not reject the rule itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides can accept the rule, because both require the judges' consent. The real difference is the litigants' consent.

steps.title: Returning to רב יהודה's rule itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to discuss רב יהודה's rule on its own: witnesses do not sign unless they know who signs with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the rule itself. רב יהודה said in the name of רב: witnesses do not sign a document, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It brings back רב יהודה's rule so it can support it with a source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the rule was only a tool for explaining the משנה. Now the גמרא studies the rule for its own sake. The word גופא signals this change.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter itself: returning to a statement quoted earlier in order to discuss it directly

phrases.aramaic: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Back to the matter itself: רב יהודה said in the name of רב:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הָעֵדִים חוֹתְמִין עַל הַשְּׁטָר כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: Witnesses do not sign on a document, etc.
phrases.notes: The "etc." stands for the rest of the rule from step 15: unless they know who signs with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the argument in the משנה and returns to רב יהודה's rule, which was quoted in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses do not sign a שטר unless they know who signs with them.

steps.title: Support from the careful people of ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רב יהודה's rule. The careful people of ירושלים would not sign, sit in judgment, or join a meal unless they knew who was with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches the same thing. This is what the careful people of ירושלים would do: they did not sign a document unless they knew who signed with them. They did not sit in judgment unless they knew who sat with them. They did not join a meal unless they knew who ate with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports רב יהודה's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the ברייתא matches רב יהודה's rule word for word. It also widens the idea: a careful person also chooses whom he judges with and whom he eats with. The part about judging fits why the judges' agreement is needed when choosing the third judge.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא also teaches this (support for a statement)

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה's rule is backed by the custom of the careful people of ירושלים, who knew their partners in signing, judging and eating.

phrases.english: A ברייתא also teaches this:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הָיוּ נְקִיֵּי הַדַּעַת שֶׁבִּירוּשָׁלַיִם עוֹשִׂין –
phrases.english: This is what the careful people of ירושלים would do:
they would not sign on a document

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יוֹדְעִין מִי חוֹתֵם עִמָּהֶן,
phrases.english: unless they knew who was signing with them,
and they would not sit in judgment

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יוֹדְעִין מִי יוֹשֵׁב עִמָּהֶן,
phrases.english: unless they knew who was sitting with them,
and they would not join a meal

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יוֹדְעִין מִי מֵסֵב עִמָּהֶן.
phrases.english: unless they knew who was reclining with them.
phrases.notes: Reclining means eating. People reclined at meals in those days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to support the rule restated in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's rule that witnesses must know who signs with them
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא describing the custom of the careful people of ירושלים

steps.title: How can a litigant reject a judge?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that each litigant may disqualify the other's judge and asks how anyone has such power.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'This one can disqualify that one's judge, etc.' Does a litigant really have the power to disqualify judges?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a new line in the משנה and questions it. It sounds strange that a litigant could simply throw out a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי מאיר in the משנה, a litigant can reject the judge the other side picked. The גמרא asks how a litigant can have that much control over a court. This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it in his power? (a phrase of surprise)

phrases.english: This one can disqualify that one's judge, etc.
Is it in his power to disqualify judges?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the side discussion about רב יהודה's rule, the גמרא returns to the משנה and starts a new topic.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling in the משנה that a litigant may disqualify the other's judge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A litigant should not have the authority to reject a judge of a court.

steps.title: Only in lay courts, not with expert judges
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן limits the rule to the lay courts of Syria, where judges were not experts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: They taught this about the lay courts in Syria, but not about expert judges.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question. A litigant can reject a judge only in the lay courts of Syria, not in a court of expert judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ערכאות שבסוריא the judges were ordinary people the litigants picked, so a litigant could refuse one. Expert judges (מומחין) carry real authority, so nobody can reject them. This explains how רבי מאיר's rule makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: the lay courts in Syria, run by non-expert judges
expert judges, recognized by the court

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
They taught this about the lay courts in Syria,
but about expert judges, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the rule applies only to non-expert lay courts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to let a litigant reject any judge at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: A litigant may reject only lay judges, never expert judges.

steps.title: The חכמים seem to show רבי מאיר spoke of experts too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן from the חכמים's words, which mention experts and imply רבי מאיר included experts.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the end of the משנה teaches: The חכמים say: When can he reject them? When he brings proof that they are relatives or disqualified. But if they were fit, or experts approved by the court, he cannot reject them. This implies that רבי מאיר was talking about experts too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יוחנן's answer. The חכמים say a litigant cannot reject expert judges, so they must be arguing with רבי מאיר, who would allow even that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the חכמים bother to say that experts cannot be rejected, it sounds like רבי מאיר said they can. That would mean רבי מאיר's rule covers expert judges, against רבי יוחנן's limit to lay courts.

keyTerms.meaning: the later part of the משנה

phrases.english: But from the fact that the later part teaches:
And the Rabbis say: When?
When he brings proof
that they are relatives or disqualified.
But if they were fit,
or experts approved by the court,
he cannot disqualify them.

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּלָל דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מוּמְחִין נָמֵי קָאָמַר!
phrases.english: This implies that Rabbi Meir is speaking of experts too!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's answer from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that רבי מאיר's rule is only about lay courts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים say experts cannot be rejected, which implies רבי מאיר holds they can, so his rule includes experts.

steps.title: Fit judges are treated like experts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the חכמים: fit lay judges count like experts, so the משנה is not discussing real experts.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: But if they were fit, they are treated like experts approved by the court, and he cannot reject them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the חכמים's words differently. They did not mention real experts; they said fit judges are like experts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'or' (או) is read as 'they become like' (נעשו כ). So the חכמים are still talking about lay judges: if they are fit, they get the same status as experts and cannot be rejected. Real experts were never under discussion, so רבי יוחנן's limit to lay courts stands.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means (a rereading of the text)
they become like, are treated like

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, rejecting a judge applies only to lay courts. Real experts can never be rejected. In the חכמים's view, even fit lay judges are treated like experts, so they can be rejected only with proof that they are relatives or disqualified.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
But if they were fit,
they are treated like experts approved by the court,
phrases.notes: Instead of 'or experts,' read it as 'they become like experts.' This one small change answers the challenge.

phrases.english: and he cannot disqualify them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 and keeps רבי יוחנן's answer from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the משנה (הכי קאמר).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים seemed to list real experts as a separate case, implying רבי מאיר included them.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים meant that fit lay judges have expert-like status. Real experts are not part of the argument, so רבי יוחנן's answer stands.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to show רבי מאיר argued about expert judges
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where the חכמים tell רבי מאיר that no one can disqualify a public expert judge. This implies רבי מאיר held that even an expert can be rejected, against רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: The חכמים said to רבי מאיר, "It is not in a person's power to disqualify a judge who is an expert for the public."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to challenge רבי יוחנן again. The חכמים in this ברייתא speak to רבי מאיר about an expert judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the חכמים had to tell רבי מאיר that an expert cannot be disqualified, then רבי מאיר must have held that even an expert can be. That contradicts רבי יוחנן, who said רבי מאיר only spoke about non-expert lay judges.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source
It is not in his power
An expert recognized for the public

phrases.english: Come and hear:
They said to Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: "They" are the חכמים who argue with רבי מאיר in our משנה.

phrases.english: It is not in his power to disqualify
a judge who is an expert for the public.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 22 defended רבי יוחנן from the משנה's wording, this brings a ברייתא with a sharper version of the same challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's limit that רבי מאיר only allows rejecting lay judges, not experts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים's reply to רבי מאיר mentions a real expert, implying רבי מאיר let even experts be rejected.

steps.title: The 'expert' in the ברייתא means a judge the public chose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: the 'expert for the public' means a judge whom the public accepted over themselves, like the lay courts of Syria. So the argument is still only about non-expert judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say it this way: It is not in a person's power to disqualify a judge whom the public appointed as an expert over themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing how we read the ברייתא's words. The 'expert' there is a judge the community chose, not a trained expert.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ברייתא is read as talking about a community-chosen judge, the חכמים and רבי מאיר argue only about such judges. This fits רבי יוחנן's claim, like step 22's answer, that a real expert is not part of the debate at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Say: read the text this way instead
Whom the public appointed as an expert over themselves

phrases.english: Say:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is telling us to read the ברייתא's words a bit differently.

phrases.english: It is not in his power to disqualify
a judge whom the public appointed as an expert over themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא: לֹא כׇּל הֵימֶנּוּ שֶׁפּוֹסֵל דַּיָּין שֶׁהִמְחוּהוּ רַבִּים עֲלֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 23's challenge by rereading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'expert for the public' meant a real trained expert, so רבי מאיר argued about experts.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means a judge the public accepted, like the Syrian lay courts, so רבי מאיר never spoke about real experts.

steps.title: רבי מאיר himself says an expert court cannot be refused
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי מאיר: a litigant may keep rejecting judges until the other side agrees to an expert court. So רבי מאיר admits a real expert court cannot be refused.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also taught in a ברייתא: A litigant may keep on disqualifying, until the other side accepts a court that is expert for the public. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up the answer it just gave. In it, רבי מאיר himself sets an expert court as the limit of disqualifying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rejecting stops once an expert court is offered, then רבי מאיר agrees that experts cannot be rejected. That is exactly what רבי יוחנן said, so his limit is supported.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way: a ברייתא supports this

steps.whatToRemember: Even רבי מאיר agrees that a real expert court cannot be refused; his debate is only about lay judges.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
He may always keep on disqualifying,
until the other accepts upon himself a court
that is expert for the public.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי: לְעוֹלָם פּוֹסֵל וְהוֹלֵךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 24's reading and רבי יוחנן's limit.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that רבי מאיר allows rejecting only non-expert judges.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי מאיר says the rejecting ends once an expert court is accepted.

steps.title: Witnesses are like experts, yet רבי מאיר lets them be disqualified
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: witnesses don't depend on the litigants' choice, just like experts. Yet רבי מאיר says each side may disqualify the other's witnesses. So why not experts too?
steps.simpleTranslation: But aren't witnesses like experts? And yet רבי מאיר said: This one may disqualify that one's witnesses, and that one may disqualify this one's witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new problem with רבי יוחנן's limit, using the משנה's rule about witnesses. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An expert judge stands on his own, not on the litigants' agreement, and witnesses also stand on their own. If רבי מאיר still lets a litigant reject witnesses, it seems he should also let him reject expert judges, against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it: opens a challenge

phrases.english: But aren't witnesses like experts?
phrases.notes: Like experts, witnesses don't need the litigants to agree to them.

phrases.english: And yet Rabbi Meir said:
This one may disqualify the witnesses of that one,
and that one may disqualify the witnesses of this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After steps 24 and 25 supported רבי יוחנן, this opens a fresh challenge from the משנה's ruling on witnesses.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's limit that, according to רבי מאיר, experts cannot be rejected.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnesses, like experts, don't depend on the litigants' acceptance, yet רבי מאיר lets them be rejected, so experts should be rejectable too.

steps.title: ריש לקיש fixes the wording: one witness, not witnesses
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says רבי מאיר could never have said a litigant can block real witnesses, so the משנה should read 'his witness' (singular).
steps.simpleTranslation: Something was already said about this. ריש לקיש said: Would a holy mouth say such a thing? Read it as 'his witness' (just one).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 26. It quotes ריש לקיש, who changes the wording of רבי מאיר's statement from 'witnesses' to 'witness.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 asked: if רבי מאיר lets a litigant reject witnesses, why not expert judges too? ריש לקיש answers that רבי מאיר never said a person can reject a proper pair of witnesses. He only spoke about a single witness, so there is no proof about experts.

keyTerms.meaning: It was already stated about this (an earlier אמורא already commented on it)
רבי שמעון בן לקיש, an אמורא from ארץ ישראל
Read the text this way (change the wording)

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not saying רבי מאיר was wrong. He is saying the words should be read differently: 'witness' in the singular.

phrases.english: It was already stated about it,
Reish Lakish said:
Would a holy mouth say such a thing?
phrases.notes: The holy mouth is רבי מאיר. ריש לקיש can't believe he would let someone block real witnesses.

phrases.english: Read: 'his witness.'
phrases.notes: Instead of 'his witnesses' (plural), read it as just one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אִיתְּמַר עֲלַהּ, אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26 by correcting the wording of רבי מאיר's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the text (plural to singular)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר lets a litigant reject a full set of witnesses, so experts should also be rejectable.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר only spoke about a single witness, so no comparison to experts can be made.

steps.title: What would a single witness be good for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this single witness is testifying for. For money he is already invalid by Torah law, and for an oath he counts fully like two.
steps.simpleTranslation: His one witness, for what? If for money, the Torah already rules him out! If for an oath, he is believed like two!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's new reading. It asks what case a single witness could be talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the witness is for collecting money, the Torah already says one witness can't make someone pay, so there is nothing to reject. If he is for making the defendant swear, the Torah itself gives one witness full power, so the litigant should not be able to reject him either way.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah (the Merciful One) already disqualified him

phrases.english: His witness, for what?
If you say for money, the Torah already disqualifies him!
If for an oath,
he is fully believed like two!
phrases.notes: One witness against a defendant obligates him to swear. For that job, one witness has full Torah power.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading 'his witness' from step 27 by asking what case it could fit.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's reading that רבי מאיר spoke of a single witness
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Either option fails: for money a single witness is already invalid, so rejecting him adds nothing. For an oath he is fully valid by Torah law, so he can't be rejected.

steps.title: The litigant had agreed to treat one witness like two
steps.stepSummary: The case is about money, where the litigant first agreed to accept one witness as if he were two, and now wants to reject him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really it is about money. It is needed for a case where he accepted him upon himself as if he were two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says the single witness is about money, in a special case where the litigant agreed to treat him like two witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally one witness can't make someone pay. But if the litigant chose to accept him like two, the question is whether he can back out. רבי מאיר says he can 'disqualify' him, meaning he may take back his agreement.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for this specific case

phrases.english: Really, it is for money.
It is needed only
where he accepted him upon himself as if he were two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 28 by narrowing the case to one where the litigant agreed to accept one witness like two.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific situation (לָא צְרִיכָא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A single witness for money has no power at all, so there is nothing to reject.
steps.terutzMaskana: The witness got his power only from the litigant's agreement, and רבי מאיר lets him take that agreement back.

steps.title: We already know from another משנה that one can back out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this teaches us, since another משנה already shows רבי מאיר lets a person retract after accepting his father or three cattle herders as judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it teaching us, that he can back out? We already learned it: If he said 'my father is trusted for me,' 'your father is trusted for me,' or 'three cattle herders are trusted for me,' רבי מאיר says he can back out, and the חכמים say he cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 29. If רבי מאיר is only saying a person can back out of an agreement, we already know that from a different משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the later משנה, a person agreed to be judged by people who are normally invalid: a relative or unlearned herders. רבי מאיר says he can retract. That is the same idea as backing out of accepting one witness like two, so why say it twice?

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next move: the גמרא must show that the case of one witness adds something beyond the case of the herders, or find another reading.
